liaisons between groups. The function returns raw and expected scores

for each group that I am studying  and only the *expected* scores per  
group (exp.grp) are given, not the raw scores by group. I thought  
maybe I'd be able to calculate the raw scores by sorting my vertices  
into groups and summing their raw scores within each group, but  
exp.grp does not seem to be the sum of exp.nli sorted by group. I have  
looked at the function code and maybe I could modify it to return the  
vbr variable - would that be the right thing to do?
I would be grateful for any help.

Manon Ragonnet.
University of Edinburgh.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

This is my first attempt with ergm and I have a couple of questions:

1. Is there any term equivalent to the edgecov() that accepts values from categorical variables? I am asking this because one of my edge list variables is "distance" (in km) of a shipment between two villages (my nodes). Distance values range from 0 to 328km (IQR=13.9), thus, I standardised this variable (and the model runs OK!). However, I am finding it very difficult to interpret the coefficient. Therefore, I decided to categorise "distance" in 3 categories (dist.c) and try to run the model with edgecov(dist.c), getting the following error:

Error in sum(c(xm)[c(xm) < 0]) : invalid 'type' (character) of argument

In addition: Warning message:

In (function (nw, arglist, ...)  : NAs introduced by coercion



2. I am also trying to interpret gwidegree. I have read Hunter 2007, Harris 2003<https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/an-introduction-to-exponential-random-graph-modeling/book237737> and checked this<https://statnet.org/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/FrequentlyAskedQuestions/gwtermsNotes.txt> and this<https://statnet.org/trac/attachment/wiki/Resources/GWDegree.xlsx> links. However, I am still a bit confused on how to interpret my results. I set my decay parameter to 0.55 (I chose this value by running the model with the fixed option=FALSE and then exponentiating the resulting coefficient: gwidegree.decay = -0.588563, thus, exp(-0.588563) = 0.55). When running the final model (see below), I get a significant (p-val=0.02) and negative gwidegree coefficient of -0.65114; aka: exp(-0.65114) = 0.521451.

mf<- ergm(netg5~edges+edgecov(netg5, attrname = "dist.s")+

             nodematch("region",diff=F)+nodefactor("region")+nodecov("fpv.s")

             gwidegree(0.55, fixed = TRUE)+mutual,

           estimate="MLE",

           control = control.ergm(seed = 1,

           MCMLE.density.guard = exp(5),

           MCMC.interval = 5000,

           MCMC.burnin = 50000,

           MCMC.samplesize = 50000)

 )



The way I am thinking of interpreting this coefficient is that my network follows a preferential attachment process. Following, I would say that [assuming that nothing else changes in the model] the odds of trade decrease by 0.52 when adding an edge between villages with low indegrees. Similarly, the odds of trade increase by 1.48 when adding an edge between villages with high indegrees... However, my network has a marked declining degree distribution (most of the villages only trade with one or two other villages, and only a few villages have a high indegree value), so my interpretation of the gwidegree term contradicts my descriptive results! Which probably means that I am very wrong somewhere. Any comments on the interpretation of gwidegree would be very welcomed!

On another note that may be relevant, my network is sparse (network density= 0.023; simplified network density= 0.008).

Thanks,

Esther Kukielka,
PhD student Graduate Group in Epidemiology,
CADMS, UCDavis.

On 08/13/2016 07:08 PM, Esther A. Kukielka wrote:
>
> Hello all,
>

> 1. Is there any term equivalent to the *edgecov()* that accepts values 
> from categorical variables? I am asking this because one of my edge 
> list variables is ?distance? (in km) of a shipment between two 
> villages (my nodes). Distance values range from 0 to 328km (IQR=13.9), 
> thus, I standardised this variable (and the model runs OK!). However, 
> I am finding it very difficult to interpret the coefficient. 
> Therefore, I decided to categorise ?distance? in 3 categories (dist.c) 
> and try to run the model with edgecov(dist.c), getting the following 
> error:
>

You can simply create dummy variables for each edge state, and pass each 
as an edgecov.  However, if you are modeling distance effects, using log 
distance as a covariate approximates an attenuated power law model (see 
e.g. Butts and Acton (2011)), which often works well and which avoids 
the granularity you will get if you treat distance categorically.  If 
you have measured distances at zero, you will want to replace those with 
a minimum effective distance if using this approach.

> 2. I am also trying to interpret gwidegree. I have read Hunter 2007, 
> Harris 2003 
> <https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/an-introduction-to-exponential-random-graph-modeling/book237737>and 
> checked this 
> <https://statnet.org/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/FrequentlyAskedQuestions/gwtermsNotes.txt>and 
> this 
> <https://statnet.org/trac/attachment/wiki/Resources/GWDegree.xlsx>links. 
> However, I am still a bit confused on how to interpret my results. I 
> set my decay parameter to 0.55 (I chose this value by running the 
> model with the fixed option=FALSE and then exponentiating the 
> resulting coefficient: gwidegree.decay = -0.588563, thus, 
> exp(-0.588563) = 0.55). When running the final model (see below), I 
> get a significant (/p-val/=0.02) and negative gwidegree coefficient 
> of*-0.65114*; aka: exp(-0.65114) = 0.521451.
>
You don't want to exponentiate the leading coefficient, since that is 
the multiplier of the GWD statistic - equation 14 of Hunter (2007).  Or, 
to put it another way, your total effect for indegree statistic i is

-0.65 * exp(-0.59)*(1-exp(0.59))^i * D_i(y)

If you plot this , you will see that it is negative for all i>0, but 
oscillates in magnitude; it is more suppressive of odd degrees than even 
degrees.  Although there could be deep reasons for this pattern in your 
data (e.g., if there are mechanisms that encourage incoming partners to 
be acquired in pairs), it could also be picking up a particular tendency 
towards in-pendant suppression.  If the GOF plots from a model without 
this term suggest that you have an anomalously low number of nodes with 
indegree 1, you may want to just try a pure idegree(1) term and see if 
that clears things up.  You might also see whether adding such a term to 
the GWD model leads you to a positive decay parameter.
>
> The way I am thinking of interpreting this coefficient is that my 
> network follows a preferential attachment process. Following, I would 
> say that [assuming that nothing else changes in the model] the odds of 
> trade decrease by 0.52 when adding an edge between villages with low 
> indegrees. Similarly, the odds of trade increase by 1.48 when adding 
> an edge between villages with high indegrees? However, my network has 
> a *marked declining degree distribution* (most of the villages only 
> trade with one or two other villages, and only a few villages have a 
> high indegree value), so *my interpretation of the gwidegree term 
> contradicts my descriptive results! * Which probably means that I am 
> very wrong somewhere. Any comments on the interpretation of gwidegree 
> would be very welcomed!
>
> On another note that may be relevant, my network is sparse (network 
> density= 0.023; simplified network density= 0.008).
>
This effect does not particularly suggest a PA process, but I wouldn't 
try interpreting it until you have the rest of the model nailed down.  
Doing the best you can with the spatial effect is particularly 
important, since such effects are often extremely powerful (and if you 
don't catch them, then most of what your dependence terms will be doing 
is trying to account for the residual spatial dependence in your data).

Hope that helps,

-Carter
